host.cpu_time_source: /proc/<pid>/stat utime+stime (10 ms ticks); ps supplies PID, RSS, and tree

notes: Terminal latency and output completion use a real PTY for both apps.
Control APIs are used only for readiness, status probes, and teardown.
Each app receives a private HOME and XDG tree; Herdr update and manifest checks are disabled during timing.
Startup is timed until an identical pane-listing probe succeeds; detached idle is sampled after one attach/detach so both servers hold exactly one pane shell.
Herdr's headless render grid is pinned to the attached geometry.
Every latency and output trial is verified against a modelled screen; a wrong or incomplete final screen fails the metric instead of scoring as fast.

Resize-storm (over the output-workload scrollback), multi-client (fresh session), pane-scaling/recovery (fresh session), and restart scenarios are reported as context; they are not folded into the balanced index.
CPU percent is one-core percentage from cumulative process CPU time, not percentage of the whole machine.
Root metrics cover server and attached client roots; cohort metrics also include their descendants.
Counts exclude .git, target, vendored code, generated bindings, translations, and preview/versioned duplicate docs.
Unsafe and unwrap counts are lexical heuristics over first-party production prefixes, not vulnerability findings.
Code size and dependency count are context metrics and do not contribute to assurance scores.

assurance.summary: First-party implementation is Rust; platform unsafe is concentrated in small PTY, process-watch, client-terminal, and detached-spawn wrappers (the added openpty shim is Android-only).

Runtime directories are forced to 0700 and both the Workspace socket and the per-Workspace control-API socket are chmod 0600 after bind, with stale cleanup that validates socket type and identity; there is no peer-credential check beyond file permissions.
Direction-specific frame caps are enforced before buffer growth, and the server bounds pending bytes, clients, accepts, and messages processed per readiness turn.

Snapshots use atomic replacement; event and catalog writes are ordered and acknowledged, with failed writes preventing unsafe checkpoint advancement. Instruction and artifact ledgers remain append-only.

The reviewed build has no self-update or background download implementation; installation is an out-of-product HTTPS-only script that verifies a published SHA-256, so there is no in-product update trust path to score.

The reviewed build has no plugin marketplace or third-party hook execution; provider detection reads declarative manifests, and external automation goes through the owner-only control API rather than in-process extensions.

Local control stays on owner-only Unix sockets; the new remote attach delegates transport and authentication to the user's OpenSSH client, and detected development URLs open only by explicit user action. No listening network control API was found.
Pane children run in dedicated process groups; event-driven retirement applies TERM, a bounded grace period, KILL, and kernel exit reaping. Runtime shutdown remains bounded.
No telemetry or analytics sender was found in first-party source or dependencies; the core crate test forbids HTTP client crates.
No first-party HTTP client or background update/manifest fetcher is present; the only socket use is a loopback liveness probe for user-detected development servers.

Workspace snapshots, event logs, the Workspace catalog, and run/instruction/artifact ledgers are persisted locally with owner-only modes and are not encrypted; the README now documents the state directory as sensitive.
Clipboard export uses OSC 52 for explicit selection/yank actions, including configured copy-on-select; file and URL actions are user initiated.
Remote attach uses the user's own SSH connection to run the remote binary; no vendor relay or cloud path is implemented.
The application has no background network feature requiring an opt-out in the reviewed build.

benchmarks.note: Time until the final marker from repeated deterministic shell output bursts becomes visible through the attached client. Every burst is oracle-checked: the ten lines above the marker must be the last ten payload lines, intact and in order.

benchmarks.name: terminal_output_ingest_rate
benchmarks.note: Known 72-byte input lines divided by visible-completion time; coalescing is allowed because final visibility is required.

benchmarks.name: client_render_output
benchmarks.note: Raw bytes emitted by the app client to the outer PTY during each output workload; lower can indicate effective damage coalescing.

benchmarks.name: resize_storm_settle
benchmarks.note: Time from the final resize of a rapid resize burst, applied to a pane holding the scrollback left by the output workload, until the pane's PTY reports the original size again through a shell probe and that probe is visible.

benchmarks.name: resize_storm_cpu
benchmarks.note: CPU time consumed by the server and client cohorts across the resize burst over the output-workload scrollback and its settle probes.

benchmarks.name: resize_storm_rss
benchmarks.note: Server plus client cohort RSS right after the resize storm settles; compare with foreground_idle_cohort_rss to see how much memory the reflow work retained.

benchmarks.name: isolated_state_size
benchmarks.note: All files in the isolated HOME/XDG benchmark tree after workloads; a context metric because products persist different semantics.

benchmarks.note: Shutdown after the one-pane latency, output, and resize workloads.

benchmarks.name: restart_ready
benchmarks.note: Restarting the stopped session with the product's own start command until the pane-listing probe succeeds. Context only: the products restore different state, so see the metadata for whether the previous burst output was visible again.

benchmarks.note: Least-squares slope of cohort RSS against pane count from one pane up to the profile pane count; each step is sampled after the new pane shell exists.

assurance.summary: Most product code is Rust, but terminal emulation crosses a large generated C ABI and first-party unsafe wrapper surface into vendored Zig Ghostty code.
Both API and client Unix sockets are explicitly reduced to owner read/write mode (0600), with stale-socket identity handling.

Client frames, initial JSON requests, graphics streams, and clipboard/image payloads have explicit size caps and private protocol version negotiation. The later stable-endpoint compatibility layer is absent from this release tag.
Session and plugin registry JSON writes use adjacent temporary files and rename, cleaning temporary files on replacement failure.

Downloaded stable binaries now require a SHA-256 from the manifest and are atomically installed, but the expected hash is delivered by the same HTTPS manifest and no independent signature verification was found.
Plugins run out of process and installs show a trust preview, but enabled plugins intentionally execute arbitrary manifest commands and hooks with user authority.
Remote attach delegates transport and authentication to OpenSSH; local control remains on owner-only sockets rather than a public TCP listener.
Unix process-group termination and Windows Job Object handling are platform-isolated, with explicit child termination and server handoff handling.
No telemetry or analytics submission was found; network features fetch product-controlled manifests and releases rather than sending usage events.

Version and agent-manifest checks are enabled by default and contact Herdr-controlled endpoints (product announcements ride on the version manifest); the benchmark disables both to remove network variance.
Session metadata and optional screen history are persisted locally as readable JSON; there is no at-rest encryption.
Clipboard/image reads are bounded and tied to explicit paste/copy interactions; remote clipboard bridging is an explicit action.
Remote access uses the user's SSH connection without a vendor relay service.
Users can disable version and agent-manifest background checks independently in configuration.
